packs.title: Groves, collections and open paths
packs.promise: Trace citrus stories, inspect living collections and make room for a short outdoor return.

q.s: Separate a specimen’s visible form from its label.
st: Enter the open museum and choose three currently displayed mineral specimens, including a worked mineral sphere if one is on view. Rotating displays may change which examples you use.
For each specimen, record an actual label name or description and one visible surface detail: a band, edge, colour change or reflected highlight.
Compare a worked sphere with another specimen’s form. If no sphere is accessible, compare two differently shaped specimens and record that limitation.
Make three small specimen cards with separate lines for label evidence and visual observation. Add one question that a label did not answer.

q.s: Let a house tour check three object guesses.
st: Join the booked tour and choose three household objects or decorative details the guide makes available in the rooms you can access. Use the first floor alone if that suits your visit.
Before reading a label or hearing its explanation, jot a tentative function for each chosen detail. Mark each guess as your own.
Use the actual tour explanation or label to check each guess. Ask one brief question at an appropriate moment if a function remains unclear; do not fill an unanswered gap with certainty.
Keep a three-row record showing the object, your guess and the confirmed explanation or remaining question. Note when a seasonal display shaped your choices.

q.s: Collect three living-collection records without collecting a plant.
st: Choose an open path with usable plant or collection labels. Read the current map or ask for directions to two nearby labelled collection areas; a full garden circuit is unnecessary.

Collect three written records from actual labels: a plant or collection name, any stated geographical origin, and the source of that information. Write “not stated” where a label does not give an origin.

Compare two visible growth forms, such as a branching shrub and an upright tree or a broad leaf and a narrow leaf. Describe visible differences without claiming a habitat adaptation the label does not establish.
Put one confirmed geographical or collection fact beside one observation for each example. End with a question about what might connect their forms with the labelled environments.

packs.title: Mission Inn Avenue and Main Street
packs.promise: Two downtown afternoons of art, architecture and close looking.

q.s: Test a material comparison in an open museum gallery.
st: Enter the admitted public galleries and choose two currently displayed artworks with usable material or medium information. They need not use the same medium.
For each, record the actual artist/title and one stated medium or material. If a label gives no medium, choose another work or ask staff where that information is available.
Find one visible mark, join, surface or edge that makes the material interesting. Compare the two works without touching or claiming a fabrication process the labels do not explain.
Make a two-column material study with label evidence, a visual detail and one unanswered making question for each work.

q.s: Let a library title hold your attention for three minutes.
st: Enter an open public collection area and choose one available book title that raises a question for you. Read the title where it is visible without disturbing another visitor.
Find a suitable public reading place and give that question three quiet minutes. Keep your phone silent; opening or borrowing the book is optional.
Write the question and one thing you noticed about how your attention behaved while you sat with it.
Leave the book where staff directs and record the displayed title as your starting point. No library card or borrowed object is part of the proof.

q.s: Turn visible building patterns into a silent sound sketch.
st: Find three visible exterior patterns from a suitable open public sidewalk view: an arch, repeated opening, decorative band or change in height.
Assign each pattern an invented sound written in words, such as a low sustained note, short repeated taps or a rising phrase. Do not perform loudly or imitate a real named musician.
Write a six-line score that brings your three sounds in and out. Mark it as your own imagined music and link each sound to its actual architectural detail.
Add a small diagram or three sentences showing where the source details sit on the facade.
